listening.title: Riverton Bus-Fare Pilot Evaluation
listening.focus: Causal limits and sampling bias in transport policy evidence
listening.script:
Maya: Hi Jonah, have you finished reading the evaluation of the Riverton bus-fare pilot for our transport policy seminar?
Jonah: Mostly. The city cut all bus fares by 50% from April to June last year to test whether cheaper fares would encourage regular commuters to switch from cars, right?
Maya: Yes, that was the official aim in the council brief — to see if lower costs would shift daily commuting patterns, not just leisure trips.
Jonah: I wrote down it ran from March to May, actually sorry, April to June — I misread the dates. Three months total. The report says weekday ridership rose 18% compared to January to March.
Maya: That's the headline increase, but we have to be careful about causality. In May, petrol prices rose 22% citywide, so driving became much more expensive during the same period.
Jonah: So we can't tell how much of the rise was due to the fare cut versus people avoiding high fuel costs.
Maya: Exactly. And there was no control group — no similar city or unaffected bus route to compare against. Without that, any causal claim is weak.
Jonah: What about the passenger survey? It said 78% of respondents would continue using the bus if fares stayed low.
Maya: But that survey was voluntary, conducted at the central terminal on weekdays. The authors note respondents were self-selected — mainly frequent riders who benefited most.
Jonah: So it overrepresents enthusiastic users and underrepresents occasional riders or those who didn't change behaviour.
Maya: Right, that's a classic selection bias. The report acknowledges the sample isn't representative of all residents.
Jonah: So for our presentation, we shouldn't say the pilot proved cheaper fares work.
Maya: No, we should conclude the evidence is suggestive but inconclusive. We can recommend a longer, controlled trial with random sampling across routes and neighbourhoods to get a clearer picture.
Jonah: That makes sense. We'll emphasize the limits and propose a better design rather than claiming success.

reading.title: Volunteer Heat Maps and Education Rankings
reading.focus: Selection bias and measurement uncertainty in policy data
reading.passage:
Cities increasingly rely on low-cost data to guide climate policy. One popular method is the volunteer heat survey, where residents use handheld sensors to record street-level temperatures during a heatwave. These campaigns generate detailed maps and raise public awareness, but they also introduce systematic errors that are often overlooked in media reports. Policymakers may be tempted to treat these maps as complete, but without understanding who participated, they risk misallocating cooling resources to already comfortable neighbourhoods.

The 2022 Riverton Heat Watch illustrates the problem. Organisers recruited 140 volunteers through neighbourhood associations and social media. Participation was voluntary, and the resulting sample was geographically skewed: 68% of readings came from the greener, wealthier northern districts, where tree cover is high and housing is less dense. Only 12% came from the industrial south, where asphalt and warehouses trap heat. Because volunteers chose where and when to measure, often near their homes on pleasant streets, the dataset overrepresented cooler areas. The published citywide average of 31.4°C therefore understated the true exposure in the hottest zones, where independent satellite data later showed peaks of 38.1°C. The example does not prove volunteers are unmotivated; it shows how self-selection shapes coverage.

The author argues that such surveys should not be dismissed, but their scope must be qualified. They are valuable for identifying relative hotspots within sampled areas and for community engagement, yet they cannot support precise citywide estimates or causal claims about the effectiveness of cooling interventions without statistical adjustment for sampling bias. The limitation is not the volunteers' effort but the lack of random, representative coverage. Weighting results by district population or supplementing with satellite data can reduce bias, but such corrections are rarely applied in initial press releases.

A similar issue of uncertainty appears in cross-country education indicators. International reports often rank countries by secondary-school completion rates, implying direct comparability. However, national definitions of "completion" differ — some count part-time vocational programmes, others do not — and data collection varies from census to sample surveys. A country reporting 89% completion may appear superior to one reporting 82%, but the gap may reflect measurement differences rather than real achievement. The passage notes that year-to-year changes within a single country, using a consistent method, are more reliable than cross-country league tables at a single point in time.

Together, these cases suggest a general principle: data collected for different purposes or through non-random methods require careful interpretation. Recognising who is missing, how definitions vary, and what comparisons are warranted prevents overclaiming and leads to more honest policy. Transparency about methods and limits, rather than precise rankings, builds greater trust in the evidence.

exercises.title: Volunteer Heat Maps and Education Rankings
exercises.focus: Selection bias and measurement uncertainty in policy data
exercises.passage:
Cities increasingly rely on low-cost data to guide climate policy. One popular method is the volunteer heat survey, where residents use handheld sensors to record street-level temperatures during a heatwave. Recognising who is missing, how definitions vary, and what comparisons are warranted prevents overclaiming and leads to more honest policy. Transparency about methods and limits, rather than precise rankings, builds greater trust in the evidence.
exercises.prompt: According to the passage, what do volunteer heat surveys provide?
options: Precise citywide temperature averages for policy
Detailed maps and public engagement despite errors
Satellite data to replace street sensors
Proof that tree cover has no effect
exercises.explanation: The passage says they generate detailed maps and raise awareness despite systematic errors. Option A claims precision the author denies.

writingPrompts.task: Task 1 · University press releases and uncertainty statements
writingPrompts.focus: selecting main trends, comparing proportions and totals, avoiding causal overclaim
writingPrompts.prompt: The table below shows the proportion of university press releases that included an explicit uncertainty statement (mentioning limitations, small sample size, or need for further research) at three universities in 2018, 2021 and 2024, along with the total number of press releases issued. Data: Northfield University – 2018: 22% of 180 releases included uncertainty; 2021: 31% of 210; 2024: 38% of 195. Westlake University – 2018: 18% of 150; 2021: 24% of 165; 2024: 29% of 170. Southridge University – 2018: 35% of 120; 2021: 33% of 140; 2024: 41% of 135. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. You should write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All data is provided here; no external information is needed.

writingPrompts.task: Task 1 · Urban wetland visitors and wildlife incidents
writingPrompts.focus: describing correlated trends, noting timing of intervention, limits of causality
writingPrompts.prompt: The chart below shows monthly visitor numbers and reported wildlife disturbance incidents at Riverton Urban Wetland Reserve from March to August 2024. In June, the reserve introduced voluntary path restrictions near nesting areas. Data: March – 8,200 visitors, 12 incidents; April – 11,500 visitors, 18 incidents; May – 15,000 visitors, 31 incidents; June – 18,400 visitors, 42 incidents; July – 19,100 visitors, 38 incidents; August – 14,300 visitors, 22 incidents. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Consider the relationship between visitor numbers and incidents without assuming direct causation. You should write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All data is provided here.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · How universities should report uncertain findings

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Balancing public access with urban wildlife protection

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Whether short pilots justify permanent policy
writingPrompts.focus: scope, seasonality and causality limits, using short-term evidence for long-term decisions
writingPrompts.prompt: A city council ran a three-month pilot closing a central shopping street to cars. Discuss the strengths and limitations of using short-term data for long-term decisions, including issues of scope, seasonality and causality. Give your own view with precise reasoning.
